In its 4 New Testament uses it is rendered either as the noun "loss" (twice, as in Acts 27:10, 21) or in the phrase "count as loss" (twice, in Philippians 3:7-8). It was an ordinary everyday word: Koine papyri use it of business losses, such as a vineyard lessee in a first-century petition pleading for a rent abatement because of the "losses" he had incurred on repairs.
prose.caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences split evenly between the two measured renderings, the second sense reflects a Greek phrase rather than a distinct meaning of the word itself.

prose.def: To suffer loss, forfeit, or be deprived of something, often as a penalty or damage incurred.
prose.article: In the New Testament ζημιόω always appears in the passive, describing someone who suffers loss or forfeits something—whether one's soul (Matthew 16:26, Mark 8:36) or, in Paul, all worldly things counted as loss (Philippians 3:8). The everyday Koine papyri sharpen the picture: there it carries the sterner sense of being fined or penalized, with one document recording a man fined fifteen bronze talents and another threatening death as the penalty. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew עָנַשׁ (5 of 6 times), which likewise means to fine or impose a penalty, so the underlying idea is loss imposed as a consequence.
prose.caution: The four measured sense labels reflect how the word is woven into translated phrases rather than four distinct meanings, and the New Testament's 'suffer loss' sense is gentler than the 'fine/penalize' force seen in the papyri.

prose.def: Zenas, a man described as a lawyer whom Paul asks to be helped on his journey.
prose.article: Zenas is a man's name appearing just once in the New Testament, at Titus 3:13, where Paul urges that he and Apollos be sent on their way well supplied. The name is probably a shortened, affectionate form of the longer Zēnodōros, formed from Zeus and the word for "gift" — the same pet-name pattern seen in names like Artemas and Olympas. Beyond the New Testament, the name turns up in a late Roman wall-scribbling at Magnesia, showing it was an ordinary name in everyday Koine.
prose.caution: This is a proper name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single reference.

prose.def: A matter being debated or investigated, especially a disputed question or point of controversy.
prose.article: ζήτημα refers to a question, dispute, or subject under inquiry—the kind of contested point people argue or investigate. It comes from the verb ζητέω ("to seek"), and fittingly it shows up only in Acts in the New Testament, always describing matters being debated (it appears 5 times). The English renderings in the digest ("question," "own," "since") mostly reflect how translators reshape the surrounding phrase rather than four distinct meanings, so the core sense stays unified. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one Oxyrhynchus document speaks of being held accountable "in any inquiry concerning unknown facts," and it could even mean a legal "claim."
prose.caution: The four "measured senses" mostly reflect different English phrasings rather than genuinely separate meanings—the word consistently denotes a question or disputed matter.

prose.def: A questioning or debate—the back-and-forth of arguing over an issue or disputed point.
prose.article: ζήτησις comes from the verb "to seek" (ζητέω) and basically means the act of inquiring, which in the New Testament shades into questioning, debating, and arguing. Its seven occurrences cluster around disputes—translators render it "dispute," "speculation," or "engaging" in debate, often something the writer views as unproductive (as in 1 Timothy and Titus). One nice detail: everyday Koine papyri use the word in a more technical legal sense, with an Oxyrhynchus petition from A.D. 186 speaking of "private suits" (ἰδιωτικῶν ζητήσεων) and official "inquiries."

prose.def: A weed that closely resembles wheat as it grows but is worthless, also known as darnel or tares.
prose.article: Ζιζάνιον refers to a weed—commonly called darnel or tares—that looks much like wheat while growing, making it hard to tell apart until harvest. prose.def: Deep darkness or gloom, the kind of thick blackness associated with a place of punishment.

The word turns up in everyday Koine: a sixth-century Oxyrhynchus papyrus has a father wanting his daughter to lead "a peaceful and quiet life," and Abbott-Smith notes that, unlike a synonym suggesting calm imposed from outside, ἡσύχιος points to tranquility coming from within.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence, so the confidence tier is low.

prose.article: θάνατος means death, and that single sense covers nearly all its uses — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "death" in 107 of its occurrences (99%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% of the time. The word stretches from the death of the body to the death of Christ, to death personified, and figuratively to spiritual death, but English almost always lands on the same word. prose.def: To look at something carefully and deliberately, to behold or watch closely with attention.
prose.article: θεάομαι means to look at something with careful, deliberate attention — more than a casual glance. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "seen" in 21 of 24 occurrences (91%), and in the New Testament Abbott-Smith notes it always carries a literal, physical sense of vision that interprets its object. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from a 2nd-century BC papyrus from the temple of Serapis at Memphis, where someone who received a vision writes that he "beheld" it, hinting at the deeper, contemplative weight the word can carry.
